body:
Why did socio-religious reform movements emerge?

During the 19th century, Indian society experienced important changes under British colonial rule. New systems of education, the growth of printing, expanding towns and contact with European intellectual ideas encouraged discussion about religion and social customs. Indian thinkers increasingly examined whether established practices were consistent with religious teachings, reason and the needs of society.

This process is often discussed in connection with colonial modernity: changes associated with modern institutions and ideas that developed under colonial conditions. British rule provided some new institutions and forms of communication, but it also involved foreign political domination and claims of cultural superiority. Indians were not passive recipients of change. They examined new ideas, defended aspects of their traditions and developed their own programmes of reform.

The social questions that reformers addressed

Reform movements arose in response to several practices and inequalities. These differed across regions and communities; no single custom was followed by every Indian.

  • Women's position: Reformers questioned restrictions on women's education, child marriage, the difficult circumstances of many widows and, in some regions, the practice of sati.
  • Caste discrimination: They criticised restrictions on social interaction, access to education and religious participation imposed through caste hierarchy.
  • Religious practices: Some questioned image worship, elaborate rituals, priestly authority and customs they believed had developed without sound religious justification.
  • Access to knowledge: They sought wider education so that people could understand religious teachings and participate in public discussion.

Social criticism was not entirely new to India. Earlier Bhakti traditions had also emphasised devotion and challenged aspects of social hierarchy. What changed in the 19th century was the growing use of printed arguments, formal associations, educational institutions and petitions seeking legal change.

Reform and revival: related but distinct approaches

Social or religious reform seeks to change practices considered unjust, harmful or inconsistent with a movement's principles. Religious revival seeks to recover or restore what its supporters regard as the original or authentic teachings of a tradition.

The distinction is useful, but the two approaches could overlap. A movement might appeal to ancient religious authority while demanding changes in contemporary society. For example, Raja Rammohun Roy drew upon the Upanishads to support monotheism and criticised sati. Swami Dayanand Saraswati called for a return to Vedic authority while opposing hereditary caste distinctions and child marriage.

How reformers tried to bring change

Different movements used several methods, often simultaneously:

  • Religious reinterpretation: They examined scriptures to challenge customs defended in the name of religion.
  • Reasoned public debate: They published arguments and responded to opponents.
  • Associations and prayer meetings: Organisations such as the Brahmo Samaj, Prarthana Samaj and Arya Samaj provided regular forums for teaching and collective activity.
  • Schools and educational societies: Education was used to extend knowledge and improve opportunities for women and other disadvantaged groups.
  • Campaigns for legislation: Reformers appealed to government authorities where they believed legal protection was necessary.

Why the distinction between law and society matters

A government could prohibit a practice without immediately removing the social attitudes supporting it. Similarly, establishing a school did not automatically make education accessible to every girl or every caste. Reformers therefore sought both institutional change and changes in public opinion.

Prelims focus

  • Socio-religious reform gained new momentum in India during the 19th century.
  • Print, education, public associations and reinterpretation of scriptures were important methods.
  • The Brahmo Samaj, Prarthana Samaj and Arya Samaj combined religious ideas with programmes of social change.
  • Revival of an earlier religious ideal could also be used to justify social reform.
  • Trap: Colonial influence was one factor in reform; Indian thinkers also drew upon indigenous intellectual and devotional traditions.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 94–100; National Institute of Open Schooling, History (315), lesson 18, Social Changes in Modern India, printed pp. 28–33, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Colonial Change and the Rise of Socio-Religious Reform

body:
Education became an area of disagreement

British administrators did not agree on what Indians should study. Some supported learning through Indian languages and classical traditions; others wanted education based mainly on European literature and sciences. These competing approaches are known as the Orientalist-Anglicist debate.

The Orientalist approach

Orientalists believed that Indian languages, legal traditions and classical texts deserved systematic study. Sir William Jones studied Sanskrit and other languages and founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal in 1784. Other Orientalist scholars included Henry Thomas Colebrooke. The Calcutta Madrasa, established in 1781, supported the study of Arabic, Persian and Islamic law.

The Anglicist approach

Anglicists argued that government-supported education should give greater importance to English and European knowledge. James Mill criticised expenditure on traditional learning, while Thomas Babington Macaulay strongly advocated English education. His Minute on Education was issued in 1835, followed by the educational decision associated with the English Education Act of 1835.

AspectOrientalistsAnglicists
Principal emphasisIndian classical learningEuropean learning
Important languagesSanskrit, Persian and ArabicEnglish
Associated figureWilliam JonesT. B. Macaulay

Wood's Despatch of 1854, issued by Charles Wood, supported a more organised system of education and the spread of European knowledge. Universities were established at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1857. These developments contributed to the growth of an educated section of Indian society that could examine both European ideas and Indian traditions.

Christian missionaries and religious criticism

Christian missionaries promoted religious instruction and established schools. Some criticised Indian religious practices, including image worship and caste discrimination. They often argued that education should develop Christian moral values rather than merely provide practical knowledge.

The East India Company initially feared that missionary activity would provoke opposition to colonial rule. The Charter Act of 1813 opened the way for greater missionary activity. Missionaries had already worked in areas outside direct Company control. At Serampore, then under Danish authority, a printing press was established in 1800 and a college in 1818.

Missionaries and Indian reformers sometimes criticised similar practices, but their aims were not identical. Missionaries could seek the spread of Christianity, whereas reformers such as Rammohun Roy and Dayanand Saraswati sought religious change from within Indian traditions. After the uprising of 1857, the colonial government became particularly cautious about openly supporting attacks on Indian religious customs.

Why printing changed religious debate

Printing made pamphlets, newspapers and books easier to reproduce and circulate. A reformer could explain an argument to readers in different places, while opponents could publish their own responses. Religious reform therefore became a subject of wider public debate rather than remaining confined to private meetings.

Rammohun Roy published Sambad Kaumudi from 1821. Orthodox opponents supported the publication of Samachar Chandrika to counter reformist arguments. This illustrates an important feature of print culture: it helped spread both demands for change and resistance to change.

The Gujarati newspaper Bombay Samachar began publication in 1822. Its appearance is an important Gujarat-linked fact in the early history of Indian-language newspapers.

English education and missionary education are not identical. Colonial educational policy addressed language, curriculum and administration. Missionary institutions could also use education to communicate religious teachings.

Prelims focus

  • 1784: William Jones founded the Asiatic Society of Bengal.
  • 1813: The Charter Act facilitated greater missionary activity.
  • 1835: Macaulay's Minute and the English education decision.
  • 1854: Wood's Despatch; 1857: universities at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras.
  • 1821: Sambad Kaumudi; 1822: Gujarati newspaper Bombay Samachar.
  • Trap: William Jones is associated with Orientalism; Macaulay with the Anglicist approach.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 7, Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation, printed pp. 81–86; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter 7, Print Culture and the Modern World, sections 6–7, printed pp. 167–170; National Institute of Open Schooling, History (315), lesson 18, sections 18.1 and 18.2, consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Print, Western Education and Missionary Criticism

body:
Rammohun Roy's central ideas

Raja Rammohun Roy (1772–1833) was a major early figure in 19th-century Indian socio-religious reform. He believed that religion should be examined through reason and moral principles. He criticised practices that he considered harmful or inconsistent with the essential teachings of Hindu religious texts.

Roy drew particular inspiration from the Upanishads, which he interpreted as supporting belief in one supreme God. He opposed image worship and elaborate ritual practices. His approach combined engagement with Indian religious learning and openness to modern education and intellectual discussion.

Monotheism is belief in one God. In the Brahmo movement, monotheism was associated with worship of a single supreme, formless divine reality rather than worship through images.

Roy's appeal to ancient texts should not be confused with an unconditional belief that every statement in the Vedas was beyond questioning. Reason and moral judgment were important to his method. This distinction becomes especially important when his approach is compared with the Vedic authority advocated by the Arya Samaj.

From Atmiya Sabha to Brahmo Sabha

Roy established the Atmiya Sabha in Calcutta in 1815. It brought together people interested in discussing religious truth and social questions. The discussions helped develop a more organised reform movement.

In 1828, Roy established the Brahmo Sabha in Calcutta. This association later became known as the Brahmo Samaj. Its worship and teaching emphasised one God, rejection of image worship and the importance of moral conduct.

The distinction between the organisations matters. The Atmiya Sabha was an earlier discussion circle; the Brahmo Sabha of 1828 marked the organised beginning of the movement generally associated with the Brahmo Samaj.

The campaign against sati

Sati referred to the burning or immolation of a widow on her deceased husband's funeral pyre. It was practised in some communities and regions, but it was not a universal Hindu practice. Roy opposed it through public arguments, pamphlets and interpretations of religious texts. He argued that widow burning lacked the compulsory scriptural sanction claimed by its defenders.

Roy also questioned the assumption that women were intellectually inferior. He argued that denying women education and then judging them as incapable was unjust. His concern for women's position extended to education and other restrictions imposed by social custom.

The colonial government, under Governor-General Lord William Bentinck, issued Bengal Sati Regulation XVII on 4 December 1829. It declared the practice illegal and punishable in territories then subject to the Presidency of Fort William. The measure was later extended to other British-controlled territories.

Distinguish the reformer from the law-making authority. Rammohun Roy campaigned against sati; Lord William Bentinck's government enacted the 1829 regulation. Also distinguish this measure from the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856, which is particularly associated with Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar's campaign.

Print as an instrument of persuasion

Roy used printed writing to communicate his ideas beyond meetings. His newspaper Sambad Kaumudi, published from 1821, became associated with public discussion of reform. Pamphlets also enabled him to present opposing arguments and answer them directly.

By using scripture, reason and print together, Roy demonstrated a method followed by later reformers: challenge a practice, explain why it should change and seek wider acceptance through public debate.

Prelims focus

  • Raja Rammohun Roy lived from 1772 to 1833.
  • 1815: Atmiya Sabha, Calcutta.
  • 1828: Brahmo Sabha, Calcutta; later known as Brahmo Samaj.
  • Roy emphasised monotheism, the Upanishads, reason and social reform.
  • 4 December 1829: Bengal Sati Regulation XVII under Lord William Bentinck.
  • Trap: The 1829 sati regulation and the 1856 widow remarriage legislation concern different practices and different reform campaigns.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 95–98; Brahmo Samaj, Brief History of the Brahmo Samaj, sections on Rammohun Roy and the founding of the movement, consulted 20 November 2026; Bengal Sati Regulation XVII of 1829, preamble and sections 1–2; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, chapter 7, Religious Reform and Public Debates, printed p. 169.]

title: Raja Rammohun Roy and the Foundations of the Brahmo Movement

body:
The movement after Rammohun Roy

After Rammohun Roy's death in 1833, the Brahmo movement experienced a period of reduced organisational activity. It gained new strength through the work of Debendranath Tagore, who helped develop its religious teaching, membership and public influence.

Debendranath established the Tattwabodhini Sabha in 1839. It promoted discussion and study of religious and philosophical ideas. The Tattwabodhini Patrika, published from 1843, became an important means of circulating religious discussion and interpretations of Indian texts.

Debendranath's work gave the Brahmo movement a more sustained organisational structure. The Tattwabodhini Sabha should nevertheless be distinguished from the original Brahmo Sabha founded by Rammohun Roy in 1828.

Keshab Chandra Sen and a wider programme of reform

Keshab Chandra Sen joined the Brahmo movement in the late 1850s. He promoted a more active programme of social reform and helped spread Brahmo ideas beyond Bengal. His concerns included caste discrimination, women's education, widow remarriage and the importance of universal moral principles.

Differences gradually emerged between Debendranath and Sen. Debendranath placed greater emphasis on maintaining continuity with the movement's religious foundations, while Sen pressed for more extensive social changes and broader religious universalism.

The Brahmo division of 1866

In 1866, these disagreements led to a formal division:

  • Adi Brahmo Samaj: Associated with Debendranath Tagore and the older section of the movement.
  • Brahmo Samaj of India: Led by Keshab Chandra Sen and associated with a more activist programme of reform.

The split did not mean that one branch supported polytheism while the other supported monotheism. Both belonged to the wider Brahmo tradition. The major differences concerned religious emphasis, leadership and the pace and extent of social reform.

Marriage reform and the division of 1878

Marriage customs were an important area of Brahmo reform. Act III of 1872 provided a civil form of marriage subject to conditions including minimum ages of 18 for men and 14 for women and neither party having a living spouse. Its original provisions were limited: neither party could profess Christianity, Judaism, Hinduism, Islam, Zoroastrianism (the Parsi religion), Buddhism, Sikhism or Jainism. It should not be understood as a general right of civil marriage for every couple regardless of religious profession.

In 1878, controversy arose over the proposed marriage of Sen's underage daughter to the young ruler of Cooch Behar. Critics believed that the proposed marriage contradicted the standards of marriage reform advocated within the movement.

This dispute contributed to the formation of the Sadharan Brahmo Samaj in 1878. Important associated leaders included Ananda Mohan Bose and Sivanath Shastri. The new organisation emphasised a more representative approach to the movement's affairs and continued its religious and social reform activities.

Remember the sequence rather than treating all Brahmo organisations as separate movements with unrelated origins: Rammohun Roy established the foundation; Debendranath strengthened the organisation; Sen promoted a more activist direction; disagreements produced later branches.

Prelims focus

  • 1839: Debendranath Tagore founded the Tattwabodhini Sabha.
  • 1843: Publication of Tattwabodhini Patrika began.
  • 1866: Adi Brahmo Samaj under Debendranath and Brahmo Samaj of India under Keshab Chandra Sen.
  • 1872: Act III provided a form of civil marriage with conditions including minimum ages of 18 for men and 14 for women.
  • 1878: Sadharan Brahmo Samaj emerged; Ananda Mohan Bose and Sivanath Shastri were important associated leaders.
  • Trap: The Sadharan Brahmo Samaj was established in 1878, not during the 1866 split.

[Brahmo Samaj, Brief History of the Brahmo Samaj, sections on Debendranath Tagore, Brahmo Samaj of India and Sadharan Brahmo Samaj, consulted 20 November 2026; National Institute of Open Schooling, History (315), lesson 18, Social Changes in Modern India, printed pp. 30–32; India Code, Act III of 1872, preamble and section 2, consulted 20 November 2026.]
